beats.beat: Mrs Hale, at the draper's window, sees Rowe and Judith return together at dusk, unchaperoned and laughing, and has the whole parish informed by morning.
Mrs Pike hears it first as triumph, assuming it confirms an attachment, then realizes with horror it is Judith spoken of, and not Louisa.
Flustered, Mrs Pike tells three separate people it was nothing at all, which naturally convinces everyone it was something.
Judith hears an invented version of the story, that she was seen weeping on Rowe's arm, from a girl at the library counter, and goes home changed in temper.
Owen Vane hears it from a customer, closes his shop early, and walks straight to the curate's lodging.

turn.note: Owen's declaration that he means to ask Rowe plainly and wants an answer before he comes home sets the whole of chapter six in motion.

continuity: Chapter 3 names a gossiping 'Mrs Copp' associated with the house; this chapter introduces 'Sarah Copp' with the same surname in a different context. Not a contradiction, but worth confirming it is meant to be the same person, or renaming one of them to avoid confusion by ear.

problems: The clause 'which was what made it so hard afterwards to fix on anybody as the inventor of the rest' is narratorial interpretation rather than a shown fact, and slows a chapter that otherwise moves briskly.

trope_note: This chapter is the engine of the chaperone's-absence trope paying off in reputation damage, and it uses the meddling matchmaker's error (Louisa/Judith confusion) to comic and consequential effect; enemies-of-manner is quiet here but still present in Judith's brisk exit lines.
fixes: The chapter runs well over target (roughly 730 words against 560). Trim the opening gossip-chain sentence ('By eight the next morning she had told the ostler at the Bell, both the Barrow girls, and a woman from Ropley...') to two listeners instead of three and drop the trailing analytic clause.
Cut the callback 'and told the girl that thread would keep' in the Mrs Pike paragraph — it restates a line already delivered in Chapter 4 and can be dropped without losing meaning.
Trim the Owen paragraph describing lozenges, fourpence, the apron and the nail — keep one or two concrete actions (shutting the door, turning the sign) rather than the full sequence.
Cut 'though she knew' from the final narrator line; the gesture of taking down his hat already tells the reader where he is going.
Consider shortening the triple 'nothing at all, nothing whatever, a wheel and a mason and no more in it than that' to two elements to tighten Mrs Pike's panic without losing the joke.
